items.title: Mapper User Guide
items.text: Welcome to Mapper — stone fabrication layout software for positioning countertop parts on slabs, pattern matching with slab photos, and exporting DXF files for CNC cutting.

items.title: What Mapper Does
items.text: Mapper helps you take countertop shapes from DXF files, place them on photos of your actual stone slabs, and arrange everything for the best pattern match. When you're done, export per-slab DXF files to send directly to your CNC saw, print labels for each part, and generate PDF reports for your shop floor.

items.title: Typical Workflow
items.text:
Import DXF → Load Slab Photos → Position Parts on Slabs → Pattern Match in Render View → Export DXF → Print Labels
  1. Import your DXF files — each DXF becomes a part (countertop piece) in the project
  2. Add your slabs — load a photo, set dimensions, crop to the stone
  3. Drag parts onto slabs — position them where you want to cut
  4. Open the Render Window — see the assembled countertop with real slab textures mapped onto each part
  5. Export — generate per-slab DXF files for the CNC, PDF reports for the shop, and labels for each piece

items.title: DXF Export
items.text: Export per-slab DXF files to send to your CNC saw. Each exported file contains the parts positioned on that slab, ready for cutting.

items.title: Exporting
items.text:
Two export options in the File menu and toolbar:

  • Export Selected Slab(s) to DXF — exports only the slabs selected in the Slab List
  • Export All Slabs to DXF — exports every slab in the project

Select a destination folder and Mapper generates one DXF file per slab.

items.title: Export Settings
items.text: Go to File > DXF Export Settings... to configure what gets included in each DXF file. The settings dialog has four tabs.

items.title: Tab 1: Text Fields
items.text:
Configure text labels that are written into each exported DXF. Each field has:

Column Description Enabled Whether this field is included in the export Name Label for your reference Format String Text with tokens like {JobId}, {PartId}, {Material} X, Y Position in the DXF file (inches) Height Text height in the DXF Rotation Text rotation angle Layer DXF layer name for this text Color ACI color index Alignment Text alignment (left, center, right, etc.)

Click Add Field to create a new text field. Select a row and click Remove Selected to delete it.

The Available Tokens panel shows all tokens you can use in format strings:

{JobId} {PartId} {JobName} {Material} {SlabNumber} {LotNumber} {Thickness} {Date} and more.

items.title: Tab 2: Trigger Labels
items.text:
Conditional labels that only appear when a part's text entities contain a matching word.

For example, a trigger label with trigger word "SINK" and output text "CUTOUT REQUIRED" will only appear on parts that contain the word "SINK" in their DXF text.

Same column options as Text Fields, plus:

  • Trigger Word — the word to search for (case-insensitive)
  • Output Text — what to write in the DXF when triggered

An empty trigger word means the label always appears.

items.title: Tab 3: Outline & Parts
items.text: Setting Description Export Slab Outline Include the slab boundary shape in the DXF Layer Name Which DXF layer for the outline Color ACI color for the outline Outline Detail Level of detail for the outline shape Line Format Line type for the outline Export Part Labels Include part label text in the DXF Text Height Height of label text Thickness Format "3cm" (metric) or "1.1811"" (inches) Include XRECORD Embed part summary metadata in the DXF

items.title: Tab 4: Filename
items.text:
Configure the output filename for each DXF:

  • Filename Template — use tokens like {SlabName}_{PartId} to build the filename
  • Character Limit — maximum filename length (0 = no limit)
  • A live preview shows what the filename will look like

items.title: Layer Conflicts
items.text: If multiple text fields or settings use the same DXF layer name with different colors, a warning appears at the bottom of the dialog in orange text. Resolve conflicts by using different layer names.

items.title: Workflow Tips
items.text:
• Configure export settings once, then they're saved for all future exports
  • Use Reset to Defaults if you want to start over
  • Check that all parts are green (Valid state) before exporting — orange or red parts may not cut correctly
  • The DXF export preserves original entity colors from the imported DXF

items.title: Label Generator
items.text: The Label Generator creates printable labels for each part in your project. Labels include part IDs, job information, material details, and a QR code — everything the shop floor needs to identify a cut piece.

items.title: Opening the Label Generator
items.text: Press Ctrl+L or go to File > Label Generator...

items.title: Interface
items.text: The Label Generator window has three main areas:

items.title: Left Panel — Preview
items.text:
• Part Preview — a large image showing the selected part on its slab, with the slab texture visible for pattern reference
  • Label Preview — shows the rendered label at its actual aspect ratio (4" x 1")
  • Edit Layout — opens the label layout editor to customize the label template

items.title: Center — Truck ID
items.text:
• Select a Truck ID from the dropdown — this identifies which truck or delivery the parts are assigned to
  • Use + to add a new truck ID, - to remove one

items.title: Right Panel — Parts List
items.text:
A table listing all parts in the project with columns:

Column Description Checkbox Select which parts to print Part ID Part identifier Material Material name (editable) Job ID Job identifier Job Name Job name Splash Checkbox — marks this part as a backsplash SubPart Checkbox — marks this as a sub-part of another piece

Click column headers to sort. Drag columns to reorder.

The footer shows counts: Parts / Splash / SubParts / Total.

items.title: Part Classification
items.text:
Parts can be classified as Part (full countertop piece), Splash (backsplash), or SubPart based on their size and shape.

  • Auto-Classify checkbox — automatically classifies parts using built-in rules
  • Reclassify All — re-runs classification on all parts

Quick-select buttons: All | None | Parts Only | Splash Only

items.title: Printing Labels
items.text:
Action Description Print Current Prints the label for the currently selected part Print All Prints labels for all checked parts in sequence (with progress bar) Export PNG Saves the current label as a PNG image file

Select a printer from the Printer dropdown before printing.

Note

Printing is currently supported on Windows only.

items.title: Customizing the Label Layout
items.text:
Click Edit Layout to open the Label Layout Editor. This is a JSON editor where you can modify the label template — changing field positions, sizes, fonts, and what data appears on the label.

Click Reset to Defaults to restore the built-in template.

items.title: PDF Reports
items.text: Generate professional PDF reports for your shop floor showing slab layouts, part tables, and assembled countertop views.

items.title: Generating a Report
items.text:
1. Go to File > Generate PDF Report... or click the PDF button in the toolbar
  2. Configure the report settings (see below)
  3. Click Generate
  4. Choose where to save the file

items.title: Report Settings
items.text: The PDF Report Settings dialog has three tabs.

items.title: Tab 1: Slab Layout
items.text:
Controls the per-slab layout pages of the report.

  • Generate Slab Layout Report — master toggle for this section
  • Page Layout:
    • One Slab Per Page — each slab gets its own full page
    • Grid Layout — multiple slabs per page in a grid (set Columns and Rows, 1–4 each)
  • Display Options:
    • Include Parts Table — adds a table listing all parts on each slab
    • Include Statistics — adds area, utilization, and waste data
    • Show Labels — shows part labels on the layout image
    • Show Text Entities — includes DXF text entities in the image
  • Slab Selection — choose which slabs to include using checkboxes, with All / None quick-select buttons

items.title: Tab 2: Render Layout
items.text:
Controls the assembled countertop view pages.

  • Generate Render Layout Report — master toggle
  • Page Layout:
    • Single Page — all parts on one page
    • By Group — parts organized by group on separate pages
  • Display Options: Show Labels, Show Text Entities
  • Part Groups — when "By Group" is selected, a grid appears where you can assign parts to named groups using the editable Group column

items.title: Tab 3: Settings
items.text:
General report settings:

Setting Description Output Mode Combined PDF (one file) or Separate Files (one per slab) Page Orientation Portrait or Landscape Company Logo Path to your company logo image (Browse to select) Disclaimer Text Text printed on each page (e.g., company info, legal notice) Disclaimer Position Where the disclaimer appears on the page Render DPI Image quality: 72 (draft), 150 (standard), 300 (high quality)

items.title: Saving Defaults
items.text:
• Set as Default — saves the current settings as the project default, so they're pre-loaded next time
  • Reset to Defaults — restores original settings

items.title: Your First Project
items.text: This walkthrough takes you from a blank project to parts positioned on a slab, ready for export.

items.title: Step 1: Create a New Project
items.text: Launch Mapper or press Ctrl+N to start a new project.

items.title: Step 2: Add a Slab
items.text:
1. Click Add Slab in the toolbar (or go to Slab > Add Slab)
  2. In the dialog that opens:
    • Click Browse Image... to load a photo of your slab (or drag the image file onto the dialog)
    • Enter the slab dimensions — Width and Height in inches
    • Set the Thickness from the dropdown
    • Give it a Name, Material, and Slab #
    • Adjust the crop rectangle on the image to frame just the stone
  3. Click Add Slab

The slab appears on the canvas with your photo cropped to the stone area.

Tip

If your slab photos are taken at a consistent photo station, see Photo Station Setup to calibrate automatic dimension scaling.

items.title: Step 3: Import DXF Parts
items.text:
1. Click Import DXF in the toolbar (or press Ctrl+I)
  2. Select one or more .dxf files from your file browser
  3. Each file is parsed and added as a part on the canvas

Parts appear as outlined shapes. If Mapper can't find a Job ID in the DXF file, you may be prompted to enter one manually.

items.title: Step 4: Position Parts on the Slab
items.text:
• Click a part to select it (it highlights)
  • Drag the selected part onto the slab
  • The part turns green when it's fully on the slab with no overlaps
  • Use Align to Axis (press A) to snap part edges flush with other parts
  • Use Common Line Cut (press C) to share a cut line between adjacent parts, saving blade kerf

See Moving & Positioning for all the ways to arrange parts.

items.title: Step 5: Check the Pattern Match
items.text:
1. Press Ctrl+R to open the Render Window
  2. Parts are shown with the actual slab texture mapped onto them
  3. Drag parts in the Render Window to fine-tune the assembled countertop appearance
  4. This is where you confirm the stone pattern looks right across all pieces

items.title: Step 6: Export
items.text:
When you're satisfied with the layout:

  • DXF Export: Go to File > Export All Slabs to DXF to generate per-slab DXF files for your CNC
  • Labels: Press Ctrl+L to open the Label Generator and print labels for each part
  • PDF Report: Go to File > Generate PDF Report for a shop-floor reference sheet

items.title: Step 7: Save Your Project
items.text:
Press Ctrl+S to save your project as a .map file. This bundles everything — slab images, part positions, and all settings — into a single file you can reopen later.

Next: Learn the Interface Overview to understand every part of the main window.

items.title: System Requirements
items.text:
• OS: Windows 10 or later (64-bit)
  • RAM: 4 GB minimum, 8 GB recommended
  • Disk: ~200 MB for the application
  • Display: 1200x600 minimum, 1920x1080 recommended

items.title: Installing Mapper
items.text:
1. Download the latest installer from the releases page
  2. Run the installer and follow the prompts
  3. Launch Mapper from the Start menu or desktop shortcut

Mapper updates automatically — when a new version is available, a notification banner appears at the bottom of the main window. Click Download to fetch the update, then Restart to Update to apply it.

You can also check manually via Help > Check for Updates.

items.title: Licensing
items.text: On first launch, the License Activation window appears.

items.title: Free Trial
items.text: Click Start 30-Day Free Trial to begin using Mapper immediately with full features. The trial period counts calendar days from activation.

items.title: Activating a License
items.text:
1. Enter your license key in the format XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX
  2. Click Activate License
  3. The window will confirm successful activation

Note

An internet connection is required for license activation and periodic revalidation. If you're offline during a revalidation check, Mapper will show a warning and try again later.

items.title: Deactivating a License
items.text: To move your license to another computer, click the small Deactivate License link at the bottom of the License Activation window. This frees the license for use on a different machine.

items.title: File Associations
items.text:
After installation, Mapper registers the .map file extension. You can:

  • Double-click a .map file in Explorer to open it directly in Mapper
  • Drag and drop a .map file onto the Mapper window to open it
  • Drag and drop .dxf files onto the Mapper window to import them as parts

items.title: Interface Overview
items.text: The Mapper window is divided into several zones. Here's what each one does.

items.title: Menu Bar
items.text:
Access all features through these menus:

  • File — New, Open, Save, Import/Export DXF, PDF Reports, Labels
  • Edit — Undo / Redo
  • View — Zoom, toggle labels/dimensions/warnings, Render Window, theme
  • Slab — Add, Edit, Remove slabs; Layout Settings
  • Part — Add Part, Remove Part, Import DXF
  • Help — Check for Updates, About

See Menus & Toolbar for a complete reference.

items.title: Main Toolbar
items.text:
Quick-access buttons for the most common actions:

New | Open | Save | Add Slab | Layout Settings | Add Part | Import DXF | Export DXF | Export All | PDF | Render | Labels

Hover over any button to see its tooltip and keyboard shortcut.

items.title: Canvas
items.text:
The large central area is your layout workspace. This is where you see slabs and position parts.

  • Left-click to select parts
  • Drag selected parts to move them
  • Mouse wheel to zoom in/out (centered on cursor)
  • Middle-click drag or Shift + left-drag to pan
  • Rubber-band selection — click and drag on an empty area to select multiple parts

Selection modes

Drag down-right for containment selection (only fully enclosed parts). Drag any other direction for intersection selection (any part the rectangle touches).

items.title: Interaction Toolbar
items.text:
A floating toolbar that can be docked to any edge of the canvas (top, right, bottom, or left). Right-click it to change the dock position or icon size (Small / Medium / Large).

It contains:

  • View toggles — Labels, Geometry Warnings, Text Entities, Auto Snap
  • Text modes — Add Text, Edit Text
  • Rotation controls — CCW/CW buttons with angle input
  • Zoom to Fit
  • Interaction modes — Measure Distance, Move by Snap, Align to Axis, Common Line Cut
  • Movement controls — Directional arrows with increment input
  • Undo / Redo

See Interaction Modes for details on each mode.

items.title: Right Panel
items.text: The right side is split into two sections, separated by a draggable divider.

items.title: Slab List (top)
items.text:
Shows all slabs in the project. Each entry displays:

  • Thumbnail image
  • Slab name, thickness, material
  • Dimensions and slab number

Click a slab to select it. Use Ctrl + click for multi-selection.

Buttons at the top: Add | Edit | Remove

items.title: Properties Panel (bottom)
items.text:
Shows details for the currently selected slab or part.

With a slab selected: Name, Material, Slab #, Lot #, Notes, area and utilization stats.

With a part selected: Job ID, Job Name, Part ID, area.

With multiple items selected: Aggregated summary (counts, combined area, utilization).

items.title: Status Bar
items.text:
The bottom bar shows:

  • Current status message
  • Total slabs and total parts (with square footage)
  • Selected part count (with square footage)
  • App version

items.title: Update Banner
items.text: When a new version is available, a banner appears above the status bar with Download and Restart to Update buttons. Dismiss it with the X button.

items.title: Adding Parts Manually
items.text: While most parts come from DXF imports, you can also create parts manually by defining a shape.

items.title: Opening the Add Part Dialog
items.text: • Press Ctrl+P or go to Part > Add Part

items.title: Defining the Part
items.text: A live preview on the left updates as you change settings.

items.title: Shape Options
items.text:
Choose from three shapes:

Rectangle

  • Set Width and Height in inches
  • Range: 0.1" to 1000"

Circle (Ellipse)

  • Set Diameter in inches
  • Creates a circular cutout

L-Shape

  • Set four dimensions: Top, Left, Right, Bottom
  • The preview shows the L-shape layout with your dimensions

items.title: Properties
items.text: Field Description Label Display name for the part Quantity Number of identical parts to create (1–50) Notes Additional information

items.title: After Adding
items.text:
Click Add Part to create the part(s). They appear on the canvas at the default position, ready to be dragged onto a slab.

If quantity is greater than 1, each part is created as a separate instance that can be independently positioned.

items.title: Importing DXF Files
items.text: DXF files are the primary way to bring countertop shapes into Mapper. Each DXF file becomes a part that you can position on a slab.

items.title: How to Import
items.text:
1. Press Ctrl+I or click Import DXF in the toolbar
  2. Select one or more .dxf files in the file browser
  3. Click Open

Each file is parsed and added as a part in the project. Parts initially appear at their DXF origin position on the canvas.

Drag and Drop

You can also drag .dxf files directly from Explorer onto the Mapper window to import them.

items.title: What Gets Imported
items.text:
Mapper reads the following from each DXF file:

  • Part outline — the closed polyline or boundary shape
  • Text entities — any text in the DXF (used for labels, Job ID extraction)
  • Layer information — layer names and colors are preserved
  • Entity colors — original DXF colors are maintained for export

items.title: Job ID Extraction
items.text:
Mapper automatically tries to find a Job ID in each imported DXF. The Job ID links the part to a specific job or order.

By default, Mapper searches for a pattern like RS-12345 in:

  • Text entities within the DXF
  • The file path
  • The filename

If no Job ID is found and Prompt when not found is enabled, a dialog appears asking you to enter one manually. You can type a Job ID or click Skip.

items.title: Job Name Extraction
items.text: The Job Name is extracted from the DXF filename using a separate regex pattern. This typically captures the descriptive part of the filename (e.g., "Smith Kitchen" from RS-12345 Smith Kitchen.dxf).

items.title: Configuring Import Settings
items.text: Go to File > DXF Import Settings... to customize:

items.title: Job ID Extraction
items.text:
• Regex pattern — the pattern to search for (default: RS\s?-?\s?\d{4,5})
  • Case insensitive — ignore case when matching
  • Search in — which sources to search (Text Entities, File Path, Filename)
  • Prompt when not found — show an input dialog when no match is found

items.title: Job Name Extraction
items.text:
• Regex pattern — applied to the filename only (extension stripped)
  • Case insensitive — ignore case when matching

items.title: Batch Import
items.text: Select multiple DXF files at once in the file picker to import an entire job in one action. Each file becomes a separate part, and Job IDs are extracted individually from each file.

items.title: Interaction Modes
items.text:
Mapper has several interaction modes that change how the canvas responds to your clicks and drags. Switch between them using keyboard shortcuts or the Interaction Toolbar.

Press Esc to return to the default Select mode at any time. Press Space to toggle the last used mode on/off.

items.title: Select Mode (Default)
items.text: The standard mode. Click to select parts, drag to move them, drag on empty space for rubber-band selection.

items.title: Align to Axis — A
items.text:
Helps you line up parts precisely. While dragging a part in this mode, Mapper snaps the part's edges to align horizontally or vertically with nearby parts.

How to use:

  1. Press A to enter Align to Axis mode
  2. Drag a part near another part
  3. The part snaps so its edges align with the other part's edges
  4. Release to place

This is useful for lining up rows of parts or aligning edges flush.

items.title: Move by Snap — M
items.text:
Point-to-point precision movement. Pick a reference point on a part, then click where that point should land.

How to use:

  1. Press M to enter Move by Snap mode
  2. Click a vertex (corner/endpoint) on the part you want to move — this is the anchor point
  3. Click the destination point on the canvas — the part teleports so the anchor lands exactly there

This is ideal for placing a part's corner exactly at a specific point on the slab or adjacent to another part.

items.title: Common Line Cut — C
items.text:
Shares a cut line between two adjacent parts, saving the width of one saw blade cut (kerf).

How to use:

  1. Press C to enter Common Line Cut mode
  2. A kerf settings popup appears below the CLC button showing the current blade and kerf width
  3. Drag a part toward another part
  4. When edges are close enough, the part snaps to share the cut edge with the kerf offset applied

items.title: Blade Presets
items.text:
The CLC popup shows the active blade name and kerf width. You can:

  • Edit the kerf width directly in the text box
  • Click the arrow to expand the blade preset list
  • Select a preset to switch blades

Different blade widths affect how close the parts are positioned to each other along the shared cut line.

items.title: Measure Distance — D
items.text:
Measures the distance between any two points on the canvas.

How to use:

  1. Press D to enter Measure Distance mode
  2. Click the first point
  3. Click the second point
  4. A result dialog shows the distance in both decimal inches and fractional inches (e.g., 24.750" and 24 3/4")

items.title: Add Text — T
items.text:
Places a text entity on the canvas.

How to use:

  1. Press T to enter Add Text mode
  2. Click where you want the text
  3. The Add Text dialog opens — enter your text, set height, color, and rotation
  4. Click OK to place it

items.title: Edit Text — E
items.text:
Modifies an existing text entity.

How to use:

  1. Press E to enter Edit Text mode
  2. Click on an existing text entity on the canvas
  3. Edit the text properties in the dialog that appears

items.title: Auto Snap
items.text: Toggle Auto Snap in the Interaction Toolbar to enable automatic snapping to nearby vertex and edge endpoints while dragging parts in any mode.

items.title: Moving & Positioning Parts
items.text: Once parts are on the canvas, you need to arrange them on slabs. Mapper provides several ways to position parts precisely.

items.title: Selecting Parts
items.text: Action Result Click a part Selects it (deselects others) Ctrl + click Add/remove from selection Ctrl+A Select all parts Click empty area Deselect all Drag on empty area Rubber-band selection (see below)

items.title: Rubber-Band Selection
items.text:
Click and drag on an empty area of the canvas to draw a selection rectangle:

  • Drag down-right → containment mode (only fully enclosed parts are selected)
  • Drag any other direction → intersection mode (any part the rectangle touches is selected)

items.title: Basic Drag
items.text:
Click and drag any selected part to move it. All selected parts move together as a group.

When you release the mouse, the move is recorded for undo.

items.title: Rotation
items.text:
Use the rotation controls in the Interaction Toolbar:

  1. Select one or more parts
  2. Set the rotation angle in the spinner (default 15 degrees)
  3. Click Rotate CCW (counter-clockwise) or Rotate CW (clockwise)

items.title: Nudge Movement
items.text:
Use the directional arrow buttons in the Interaction Toolbar to move selected parts by a precise increment:

  1. Set the move increment in the spinner (default in inches, 0.125" steps)
  2. Click North, South, East, or West

items.title: Interaction Modes
items.text:
For more advanced positioning, switch to one of the Interaction Modes:

  • Align to Axis (A) — snap edges to other parts
  • Move by Snap (M) — point-to-point precise placement
  • Common Line Cut (C) — share cut lines between parts

items.title: Deleting Parts
items.text: Select parts and press Del or go to Part > Remove Part.

items.title: Part States & Colors
items.text: Every part on the canvas is color-coded to show its current state. This gives you instant visual feedback about whether parts are correctly placed.

items.title: State Colors
items.text: Color State What It Means Grey Free The part is not on any slab Green Valid The part is fully on a slab with no overlaps — ready to cut Yellow Overlap The part is on a slab but overlapping another part Orange Off Slab The part is partially outside the slab boundary Red Off Slab + Overlap The part is partially off the slab AND overlapping another part Grey (darker) Locked The part is locked in place and cannot be moved

items.title: What to Aim For
items.text:
Every part should be green (Valid) before export. This means:

  • The part is completely within the slab boundary
  • It doesn't overlap any other part
  • There's room for the saw kerf between parts

items.title: How States Update
items.text:
Mapper recalculates part states automatically whenever you:

  • Move a part
  • Add or remove a part
  • Add or remove a slab
  • Change slab dimensions

During drag operations, collision detection runs at up to 60 times per second so you get real-time feedback.

items.title: Geometry Warnings
items.text: Toggle Show Geometry Warnings in the Interaction Toolbar (or View > Show Geometry Warnings) to display visual warning overlays on parts that have collision issues.

items.title: Tips
items.text:
• If a part is orange, try nudging it inward — it may be just slightly past the slab edge
  • If a part is yellow, drag it away from the overlapping part or use Common Line Cut to share the edge properly
  • Grey (Free) parts need to be dragged onto a slab before they can be exported
  • Check that all parts are green before running DXF export

items.text: Item Shortcut Description Add Part Ctrl+P Manually create a new part Remove Part Del Delete selected part(s) Import DXF... Ctrl+I Import DXF files as parts

items.title: Help Menu
items.text: Item Description Check for Updates... Check for a newer version of Mapper About Mapper Show version and application information

items.title: Main Toolbar
items.text:
Left to right:

Button Action Shortcut New New Project Ctrl+N Open Open Project Ctrl+O Save Save Project Ctrl+S Add Slab Open Add Slab dialog — Layout Settings Open Slab Layout Settings — Add Part Create a manual part Ctrl+P Import DXF Import DXF files Ctrl+I Export DXF Export selected slabs to DXF — Export All Export all slabs to DXF — PDF Generate PDF Report — Render Open Render Window Ctrl+R Labels Open Label Generator Ctrl+L

items.title: Interaction Toolbar
items.text: See Interaction Modes for detailed descriptions of each mode and control.

items.title: Render Window
items.text: The Render Window shows the assembled countertop with real slab textures mapped onto each part. This is where you verify that the stone pattern flows correctly across all pieces before committing to a cut.

items.title: Opening
items.text: Press Ctrl+R or go to View > Render Window or click Render in the toolbar.

items.title: What You See
items.text:
Each part is displayed with the actual slab photo texture clipped and rotated to match where it sits on the slab. The result is a realistic preview of what the assembled countertop will look like after cutting and installation.

Parts also show their outlines, and optional overlays like labels, dimension callouts, text entities, and collision state colors.

items.title: Canvas Interaction
items.text:
The Render Window canvas works like the main layout canvas:

Action Result Click a part Select it Ctrl + click Multi-select Drag on empty area Rubber-band selection Drag a selected part Move it (render position only) Middle-click drag or Shift + drag Pan the view Mouse wheel Zoom in/out

Important

Moving parts in the Render Window changes their render position only — it does not affect where they're cut from the slab (the layout position). This lets you adjust the assembled appearance without changing the cutting layout.

items.title: Interaction Modes
items.text:
The same modes are available as in the main canvas:

Key Mode A Align to Axis M Move by Snap C Common Line Cut Esc Select mode

The status bar at the bottom shows the current mode and a reminder of the shortcuts.

items.title: Toolbar
items.text:
The Render Window toolbar provides:

  • Toggle Labels — show/hide part labels
  • Toggle Text Entities — show/hide DXF text on parts
  • Text Color — switch between Black, White, or DXF Original text color
  • Toggle Collision Warnings — show/hide collision state colors
  • Rotation — CCW/CW buttons with angle input
  • Zoom to Fit — fit all parts in view
  • Mode toggles — Align to Axis, Move by Snap, Common Line Cut
  • Movement — directional nudge buttons with increment input
  • Z-Order — Bring to Front / Send to Back (controls which part draws on top when overlapping)
  • Undo / Redo — undo render position changes
  • Reset — reset selected part to its DXF original position
  • Reset All — reset all parts to their DXF original positions

items.title: Z-Order
items.text: When parts overlap in the render view, use Bring to Front and Send to Back to control which part appears on top. This is purely visual — it affects the render preview and PDF reports.

items.title: Part Groups
items.text: Groups let you organise parts for the PDF render report. Each group gets its own page in the report, printed in panel order, with any ungrouped parts collected on a final page.

items.title: Groups Panel
items.text:
Click Groups in the toolbar (or View > Groups) to open the Groups panel in the right dock.

  • New Group — creates a new group and auto-names it ("Group 1", "Group 2", …). If parts are selected they are assigned to the new group immediately. Rename the group afterwards by double-clicking its name.
  • Rename — double-click a group name to edit it inline.
  • Colour swatch — click the swatch next to a group name to cycle to the next palette colour. That colour is used for canvas overlays (outlines and badges).
  • ⋯ menu — each group row has an overflow menu with:
    • Add selected parts — assign the currently selected parts to this group
    • Remove selected parts — remove the currently selected parts from this group
    • Select parts — select all parts that belong to this group on the canvas
    • Highlight parts — flash the group's parts on the canvas so you can identify them at a glance
    • Move Up / Move Down — reorder groups; this controls the page order in the PDF report
    • Delete group — removes the group; parts are never deleted

items.title: Assigning Parts
items.text:
Right-click any part on the canvas to assign or unassign it:

  • Add to group → — shows a submenu of existing groups; pick one to assign the part
  • Remove from group — removes the part from whichever group it currently belongs to (always shown; disabled when the part is not in any group)

A part can belong to at most one group at a time.

items.title: Canvas Overlays
items.text: Click Show Groups in the toolbar to toggle coloured overlays on the canvas. When enabled, each part belonging to a group is drawn with a coloured outline and a small badge in its assigned group colour.

items.title: Undo
items.text: All group changes — creating, renaming, recolouring, reordering, adding/removing parts, and deleting groups — are fully undoable with Ctrl+Z.

items.title: Resetting Positions
items.text:
If you've moved parts in the Render Window and want to start over:

  • Reset Selected — go to Part > Reset Selected to DXF Original or click the Reset toolbar button
  • Reset All — go to Part > Reset All to DXF Original or click the Reset All toolbar button

This restores each part's render position to where it was originally defined in the DXF file.

items.title: Adding a Slab
items.text: Slabs represent the physical stone slabs you'll cut parts from. Each slab has dimensions, a photo (optional but recommended), and metadata.

items.title: Opening the Add Slab Dialog
items.text:
• Click Add Slab in the toolbar
  • Or go to Slab > Add Slab in the menu

items.title: Loading a Slab Photo
items.text:
You have two options:

  1. Browse — click Browse Image... to open a file picker
  2. Drag and drop — drag an image file directly onto the dialog

Supported formats: JPG, PNG, BMP, and other common image types.

Once loaded, the photo appears in the left panel with a crop rectangle overlay.

items.title: Cropping the Photo
items.text:
The crop rectangle defines which part of the photo represents the stone. Drag the handles to adjust.

  • Corner handles — resize the crop area
  • Edge handles — resize one dimension
  • Inside the rectangle — drag to reposition

items.title: Fine Adjustment
items.text:
Use the buttons below the image for precision:

  • Move — shift the crop Left / Right / Up / Down
  • Resize — Decrease / Increase crop size
  • Reset — return to the full image

Corner Magnification

Check Corner Magnification to see a zoomed-in view of each crop corner. This helps you align the crop precisely to the slab edges.

Keyboard shortcuts in the crop dialog: Ctrl+Left / Ctrl+Right / Ctrl+Up / Ctrl+Down to move, ++ctrl+num-subtract++ / ++ctrl+num-add++ to resize.

items.title: Setting Slab Properties
items.text:
On the right side of the dialog:

Field Description Name A label for this slab (e.g., "Kitchen Island Slab") Material Stone type (e.g., "Calacatta Gold") Slab # Identifier number for the slab Lot # Lot or bundle number Thickness Select from the dropdown (e.g., 2cm, 3cm) Width Slab width in inches Height Slab height in inches Quantity Number of identical slabs to add (1–99) Notes Any additional information

items.title: Slab Shapes
items.text:
Choose a shape in the dialog:

  • Rectangle — standard rectangular slab (width and height)
  • L-Shape — an L-shaped slab defined by four dimensions (Top, Left, Right, Bottom)

Note

Shape selection is only available when adding a new slab, not when editing.

items.title: Auto-Parsing from Filename
items.text:
If your slab photos follow a naming convention (e.g., 3cm Quartz #1 - 126.5x63.jpg), Mapper can automatically extract the thickness, material, dimensions, slab number, and lot number from the filename.

When a file is loaded, the Auto-Parsed from Filename section shows what was extracted. Click Configure... to customize the parsing patterns. See Filename Parsing for details.

items.title: After Adding
items.text: The slab appears on the canvas at the next available position in the grid layout. If you added multiple slabs (Quantity > 1), they are each placed in sequence.

items.title: Auto-Crop
items.text: Auto-Crop uses computer vision to automatically detect the slab outline in your photo and fit the crop rectangle to it. This saves time compared to manually adjusting crop handles.

items.title: Using Auto-Crop
items.text:
In the Add Slab or Edit Slab dialog, once an image is loaded:

  1. Configure the detection settings (see below)
  2. Click Auto Crop
  3. Mapper analyzes the image and adjusts the crop rectangle to the detected slab edges
  4. Fine-tune the result manually if needed

Click Clear to remove the detected outline overlay.

items.title: Detection Settings
items.text:
Setting Description Background Mode How the background is identified — choose based on your photo setup Detail Level Controls sensitivity of edge detection. Higher detail catches more edges but may include noise Outline Mode How the detected outline is used to set the crop rectangle

Tip

Experiment with the settings to find what works best with your photo setup. Consistent lighting and a contrasting background (darker or lighter than the stone) give the best results.

items.title: Scale Modes
items.text: After auto-crop detects the outline, choose how dimensions are determined:

items.title: Scale to Slab Size
items.text: The crop is mapped to the Width and Height values you entered manually. The crop rectangle is adjusted to match the slab's aspect ratio.

items.title: Photo Station
items.text:
If you have a calibrated photo station (consistent camera position and distance), Mapper can calculate the slab dimensions automatically from the pixel measurements.

Select Photo Station and the dimensions are computed using your saved scale factors. See Photo Station Setup to calibrate.

items.title: Tips for Best Results
items.text:
• Use consistent, even lighting on the slab
  • A background that contrasts with the stone color works best
  • Keep the camera at the same height and angle for every photo
  • Avoid shadows across the slab edges
  • If auto-crop misses an edge, adjust manually and note what background mode worked

items.title: Editing Slabs
items.text: After adding a slab, you can modify its properties and image at any time.

items.title: Opening the Edit Dialog
items.text:
• Select a slab in the Slab List (right panel), then click Edit
  • Or go to Slab > Edit Slab...
  • Or double-click a slab in the list

Note

Edit Slab is only available when a single slab is selected.

items.title: What You Can Change
items.text:
The Edit Slab dialog is the same as the Add Slab dialog, with these differences:

  • Shape and Quantity fields are hidden (you can't change the shape after creation)
  • All other fields are editable: Name, Material, Slab #, Lot #, Thickness, Width, Height, Notes
  • You can load a new photo or adjust the crop

items.title: Editing in the Properties Panel
items.text:
For quick changes, you can also edit slab properties directly in the Properties Panel (right side of the main window):

  • Name, Material, Slab #, Lot #, Notes are all editable inline
  • Area and utilization stats are displayed read-only

items.title: Removing Slabs
items.text:
1. Select one or more slabs in the Slab List
  2. Click Remove in the Slab List header, or go to Slab > Remove Slab

Warning

Removing a slab does not delete the parts that were on it — they become "Free" (grey) parts and remain in the project.

items.title: Multi-Slab Selection
items.text:
When multiple slabs are selected, the Properties Panel shows an aggregated summary:

  • Count of selected slabs
  • Materials list
  • Total parts across all selected slabs
  • Combined area, used area, waste area
  • Overall utilization percentage

items.title: Filename Parsing
items.text: If your slab photos follow a naming convention, Mapper can automatically extract properties from the filename when you load an image in the Add Slab dialog.

items.title: Example
items.text:
A filename like 3cm Calacatta Gold #1 - 126.5x63.jpg can be parsed into:

  • Thickness: 3cm
  • Material: Calacatta Gold
  • Slab #: 1
  • Width: 126.5
  • Height: 63

items.title: Configuring Patterns
items.text:
In the Add Slab dialog, click Configure... in the Auto-Parsed from Filename section. This opens the Slab Filename Parsing dialog.

Each property has its own regex pattern with named capture groups:

Field Capture Group(s) Dimensions width, height Thickness value Material value Slab # value Lot # value Name If blank, uses the remaining text after other fields are extracted

Check Case Insensitive if your filenames have inconsistent capitalization.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
The bottom half of the dialog has a live test area:

  1. Type a filename in the Test Filename box
  2. The parsed results update immediately below
  3. Validation errors appear in red if a pattern doesn't match

This lets you fine-tune patterns against real filenames before saving.

items.title: Tips
items.text:
• Start with the defaults and adjust only if your naming convention differs
  • The dimensions pattern is usually the most important — make sure it captures your width/height format
  • Use Reset Defaults if you get lost and want to start over
  • Patterns are saved per-machine and apply to all projects

items.title: Layout Settings
items.text: Layout Settings control how slabs are arranged on the canvas when you add new slabs or relayout existing ones.

items.title: Opening Layout Settings
items.text:
• Click the grid icon in the toolbar
  • Or go to Slab > Layout Settings...

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Setting Description Grid Style The arrangement pattern for slabs Columns Per Row How many slabs fit in each row (1–10) Horizontal Spacing Gap between slabs side-by-side, in inches Vertical Spacing Gap between rows of slabs, in inches Start X Horizontal offset for the first slab, in inches Start Y Vertical offset for the first slab, in inches

A live preview on the right side of the dialog shows how your settings will arrange the slabs.

items.title: Applying
items.text:
Click Apply to save and relayout all slabs with the new settings. Click Cancel to discard changes.

Use Reset to Defaults to return to the original settings.

items.title: Relayout All Slabs
items.text:
You can also relayout slabs at any time without opening the dialog — go to Slab > Relayout All Slabs. This applies the current layout settings to reposition every slab on the canvas.

Note

Relayout repositions the slabs themselves. Parts stay at their world positions, so if a slab moves, the parts that were on it may no longer overlap. You'll need to reposition parts after a relayout.

items.title: Photo Station Capture
items.text:
Photo Station Capture drives a tethered Canon camera to photograph slabs, fills in the job details, and saves a JPG plus a metadata file that Mapper can read back later. It replaces walking a memory card back and forth between the photo station and the mapping PC.

Not the same as Photo Station calibration

This page covers the camera capture window. If you're looking for the pixels-to-inches calibration used by Auto-Crop, see Photo Station Setup instead — that's a separate, older feature with the same name for the same physical setup (a fixed camera position), but it doesn't involve a tethered camera.

items.title: Camera Setup
items.text:
Photo Station Capture is built for Canon cameras (tested with the EOS R100; other EDSDK-compatible Canon bodies should also work).

  1. Connect the camera to the PC with a USB cable
  2. Turn the camera on
  3. Open Photo Station (see below) — it detects the camera automatically

You don't need to insert or format an SD card for this workflow: photos download directly to the PC and are never written to the card.

If the camera is turned on after the window is already open, it's detected automatically — there's no reconnect button to press. If the camera goes to sleep or is unplugged mid-session, Photo Station shows Waiting for camera… and reconnects on its own once it's available again; nothing you've already shot is lost.

items.title: Integrated vs Standalone
items.text:
Photo Station runs in two forms:

  • Integrated — a window inside Mapper, for shops that photograph and map on the same PC. Open it from View > Photo Station.... Saved photos can be imported straight into the open project as a new slab.
  • Standalone — a separate, lightweight installer for a dedicated photo-station PC (e.g., in the fabrication shop, away from the mapping computer). It only does capture, form entry, save, and label printing — no DXF, no layout.

items.title: Standalone Licensing
items.text: The standalone app requires a license key on first launch, but it's not a second license — enter the same key you already use for Mapper. Activating Photo Station Capture does not consume one of your Mapper seats; it's tracked separately on the license server specifically so a shop can run a dedicated photo station without buying an extra seat.

items.title: Opening Photo Station
items.text:
• Integrated: the Photo Station button on the main toolbar, or View > Photo Station... in the main menu
  • Standalone: launch the Mapper Photo Station app directly

The window (or app) stays open across sessions the same way the Render Window does — closing it with the X hides it; it reopens instantly next time rather than restarting the camera connection from scratch.

Standalone window opens maximized

The standalone app opens maximized on launch (minimum size 900x600), so it fills a shop-PC monitor without you needing to resize it. Un-maximize any time if you'd rather run it in a smaller window.

Live view looks too dark?

The first time you open Photo Station, a one-time tip reminds you to open your camera's menu and set Exposure Simulation to Disable if the live preview looks unusually dark. This only affects what you see on screen — your saved photos keep their normal exposure either way. Check "Don't show this again" to dismiss it for good.

items.title: Form Fields
items.text:
Field Required Notes Job Name Yes Upper-cased automatically in the saved filename Stone Color Yes Title-cased automatically in the saved filename Thickness Yes Dropdown — options editable in Settings Length No In inches; appears in the filename only when Height is also filled in Height No In inches; appears in the filename only when Length is also filled in Material No Dropdown — options editable in Settings Slab # No Omitted from the filename if blank

Job Name, Stone Color, and Thickness are required to save a photo or print a label — you can print a label from the form alone, without taking a photo first.

items.title: Live View, Take, and Retake
items.text:
While the camera is connected and you haven't just taken a shot, the preview panel shows a live feed from the camera, marked with a LIVE VIEW badge in the top-left corner so you always know you're looking at the live stream rather than a captured photo. Press TAKE PHOTO (or Enter) to capture — the shot appears in the preview and is added to the session's history strip (the vertical filmstrip to the right of the preview).

  • Click any thumbnail in the filmstrip to review that shot (this is what Save will use)
  • Double-click a thumbnail to open it full-size in a popup — scroll the mouse wheel to zoom in/out (centered on the cursor), drag to pan, double-click the popup or click Fit to reset, Escape or Close to dismiss. Handy for checking focus or pattern detail before you move on
  • Click Back to live to return to the live feed and take another shot
  • Reset clears the whole session's shots and form fields

If a capture doesn't come back within about 10 seconds, Photo Station shows a timeout error and returns to live view — check the cable and try again.

items.title: Save Behavior
items.text:
There are two save buttons, both acting on the currently-selected shot:

Button Clears Use when Save & Next Slab Only Length, Height, and Slab # Shooting a batch of slabs for the same job and stone — Job Name, Stone Color, Material, and Thickness stay filled in Save & Clear Every field Moving on to a different job or stone

Slab # is always left blank after saving rather than auto-incremented — slabs are often shot out of numeric order, so Mapper doesn't guess at the next number.

Either button writes the currently-selected shot as a JPG using your filename template (see below). If a file with that name already exists, Mapper adds (2), (3), etc. — it never overwrites an existing photo.

Clear filmstrip on save (checkbox above the save buttons, on by default): after a successful save, the entire filmstrip is cleared — not just the saved shot — so an old photo can't be saved for the next slab by mistake. Untick it if you deliberately shoot several slabs before saving any of them; saving then removes only the selected shot and keeps the rest.

items.title: Filename Templates
items.text:
The saved filename is built from a template of {Token} placeholders, editable in Settings (see below). The default template is:

{JobName} - {Thickness} {StoneColor}[ #{SlabNumber}][ - {Length}x{Height}]

which produces names like SMITH KITCHEN - 3cm Calacatta Gold #2 - 130x78.jpg.

Square brackets [ ... ] mark an optional group: everything inside — including spaces, #, or - — is dropped together whenever any token inside it is empty. That's why the slab-number and dimensions portions disappear cleanly from the name instead of leaving a stray # or -.

Token Value {JobName} Upper-cased {StoneColor} Title-cased {Material} As selected in the dropdown {Thickness} As selected in the dropdown {SlabNumber} Blank if not entered {Length} / {Height} In inches; blank if not entered {Date} yyyy-MM-dd, at save time {Time} HHmmss, at save time

Dimensions are all-or-nothing

The [ - {Length}x{Height}] group only appears when both Length and Height are filled in — entering just one drops the whole segment from the filename (the value you did enter is still saved if you're writing a sidecar, just not reflected in the name).

items.title: JSON Sidecar (off by default)
items.text:
Mapper can optionally write a matching .json "sidecar" file alongside the JPG (metadata: job, color, material, thickness, slab #, dimensions, capture time, camera model). As of this version, the sidecar is off by default — turn it on in Settings if you want it.

Why you'd want it on: it's what lets Add Slab on the mapping PC prefill the name, material, thickness, and dimensions automatically when you load a saved photo. Without it, Add Slab falls back to parsing the filename instead — which recovers job name, stone color, and dimensions (if your template includes them), but not Material, since there's no filename-parse equivalent for it. If you want Material to prefill without the sidecar, add {Material} to your filename template so it's at least visible in the name for reference.

Where photos are saved:

  • Integrated: a Photos subfolder next to your .map project file. If the project hasn't been saved yet, photos go to the default folder configured in settings instead.
  • Standalone: the folder configured in the app's Settings dialog — typically a synced folder (OneDrive or similar) that's also reachable from the mapping PC.

Cross-PC workflow: if you shoot on a standalone photo-station PC and map on a different PC, point the standalone save folder at a folder that syncs to (or is shared with) the mapping PC. If the sidecar is turned on, once the JPG and its .json file arrive there, opening that photo in Add Slab on the mapping PC prefills the fields automatically — this is the entire integration between the two machines. With the sidecar off, filename parsing does the same job for whichever fields your template includes.

Tip

Add Slab reads a sidecar for any image you load, not just ones saved from Photo Station — as long as a .json file with the same name sits next to the .jpg.

items.title: Save on the Integrated Window
items.text:
When Photo Station is running inside Mapper, either save button does both of the following:

  1. Writes the JPG (and sidecar, if enabled) to the Photos folder, exactly as standalone does — this is your permanent record
  2. Opens the normal Add Slab dialog for that photo, pre-filled from the form, so you can crop and add it to the open project right away

items.title: Label Printing
items.text:
Click Print Label to print a 4"x3" label (at 300 DPI) with the job name, stone color, material, thickness, dimensions, slab number, date, and a QR code encoding the same metadata as the sidecar. It works with just the form filled in — a photo isn't required.

Set the printer used in Settings (standalone) or your usual print settings (integrated).

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Thickness / Material options — comma-separated lists, editable in the Settings dialog (standalone) or the app's settings (integrated)
  • Save Path — the default photo/sidecar folder
  • Printer — which printer label prints go to
  • Filename Template — the token template used to name saved photos (see Filename Templates above), with a live example preview underneath the field so you can check your changes before saving. Leaving it blank restores the default template
  • Also write a .json sidecar next to each photo — checkbox, off by default (see JSON Sidecar above)

Where to find Settings: in the standalone app, File > Settings; in the integrated window, the Settings button in the top-right corner. Both open the same dialog. On the integrated window, the Save Folder is only a fallback used while the project hasn't been saved yet — once it has, photos always go to the Photos folder next to the project file.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
Camera not detected

  • Confirm the USB cable is connected and the camera is powered on
  • Try a different USB port or cable
  • Make sure no other application (including Canon's own EOS software) is already connected to the camera — EDSDK cameras can only be controlled by one application at a time
  • Restart Photo Station if the camera was plugged in before the app started and still isn't showing as connected

Photos aren't prefilling in Add Slab

  • Check whether the sidecar checkbox is turned on in Settings — it's off by default, so if you haven't enabled it, prefill is coming entirely from filename parsing, and Material won't prefill (add {Material} to your template if you need it visible)
  • If the sidecar is on, check that both the .jpg and its matching .json file made it to the folder you're loading from — if only the photo synced (some sync tools can lag on small files, or a firewall/AV tool may have blocked one), the prefill data won't be there
  • The sidecar must have the same filename as the photo (just a different extension) and must not have been renamed independently of it

Save fails with a folder error

  • For the integrated window: save the project first, or set a default photo folder in settings
  • For standalone: set a save folder in the Settings dialog before saving

items.title: Photo Station Setup
items.text:
If your shop has a photo station — a fixed camera position where you photograph every slab — you can calibrate Mapper to automatically calculate slab dimensions from photos.

Not the same as Photo Station Capture

This page covers the pixels-to-inches calibration used by Auto-Crop. If you're looking for the tethered Canon camera window that photographs slabs and saves them with metadata, see Photo Station Capture instead.

items.title: How It Works
items.text:
Photo Station calibration establishes a pixels-to-inches ratio. Once calibrated, Mapper converts the pixel dimensions of the detected crop area into real-world inches.

The formula is simple: inches = pixels x scale factor

items.title: Calibrating
items.text:
1. Open the Add Slab dialog and load a photo
  2. In the Auto-Crop section, select the Photo Station radio button
  3. Click Calibrate...

The Photo Station Calibration dialog opens with two sections:

items.title: Current Scale Factors
items.text: Shows the current Scale X and Scale Y values (pixels to inches). These are what Mapper uses for conversion.

items.title: Calibration Helper
items.text:
To calibrate, you need a reference object of known size in your photo (or a slab with known dimensions):

  1. Known Width — enter the real width in inches of your reference object
  2. Measured Width — enter the width in pixels as measured in the photo
  3. Click Apply X to set the horizontal scale factor

Repeat for height:

  1. Known Height — enter the real height in inches
  2. Measured Height — enter the height in pixels
  3. Click Apply Y to set the vertical scale factor

Or click Apply Both Calculated Scales to set both at once.

Tip

For best accuracy, use the largest reference object available (ideally a slab with known dimensions). Measure edge-to-edge in pixels using the crop rectangle's pixel readout.

items.title: After Calibration
items.text:
Once calibrated, any time you use Auto-Crop with Photo Station mode selected, the slab dimensions (Width and Height) are calculated automatically. You don't need to type them in manually.

The calibration values are saved and persist across sessions. Recalibrate if you move the camera or change the photo station setup.
